hook: For forty-five years, the world champion lost roughly one game every six years. In checkers.
story: His name was Marion Tinsley. He won nine world championship matches and never lost one; his opponents gave up trying to beat him and played for draws. He got bored and quit for twelve years. So in 1990 they sat him across from a computer called Chinook, a machine searching twenty moves ahead. On the tenth move of the tenth game, the machine liked its position. Tinsley looked up and told the programmer he was going to regret that move.
number: He wasn't guessing. His notes show he'd seen the end of the game at move eleven; the machine would have needed to search sixty moves ahead to know it had already lost. By most counts, Marion Tinsley lost seven games in forty-five years, which makes him the greatest checkers player of all time.
closer: The computer took his title in 1994, without winning a single game of the match.
full_text: For forty-five years, the world champion lost roughly one game every six years. In checkers. His name was Marion Tinsley. He won nine world championship matches and never lost one; his opponents gave up trying to beat him and played for draws. He got bored and quit for twelve years. So in 1990 they sat him across from a computer called Chinook, a machine searching twenty moves ahead. On the tenth move of the tenth game, the machine liked its position. Tinsley looked up and told the programmer he was going to regret that move. He wasn't guessing. His notes show he'd seen the end of the game at move eleven; the machine would have needed to search sixty moves ahead to know it had already lost. By most counts, Marion Tinsley lost seven games in forty-five years, which makes him the greatest checkers player of all time. The computer took his title in 1994, without winning a single game of the match.
